label: Toxicology
blurb: Antidotes, poisonings, overdose management, and chelation therapy

drugs.name: N-Acetylcysteine
drugs.primaryEffect: Prevents hepatic necrosis from acetaminophen
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acetaminophen overdose, non-acetaminophen acute liver failure, contrast nephropathy prevention, mucolytic therapy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Acts as a cysteine donor to regenerate hepatic glutathione, which conjugates the toxic metabolite NAPQI, and also directly substitutes for glutathione in detoxifying it.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea and vomiting, anaphylactoid reaction with rapid intravenous loading, flushing, bronchospasm, rash
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in acetaminophen toxicity; slow or pause the infusion for anaphylactoid reactions rather than stopping treatment
drugs.tooltip: Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram for a single acute ingestion with a known time. Most effective within 8 hours but still worth giving beyond 24 hours in established hepatotoxicity.

drugs.name: Naloxone
drugs.primaryEffect: Immediately reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression
drugs.treatmentUsage: Opioid overdose, reversal of iatrogenic opioid sedation, take-home overdose kits, undifferentiated coma with pinpoint pupils
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitive antagonist with very high affinity at the mu opioid receptor, displacing agonists and restoring central respiratory drive within minutes.
drugs.sideEffects: Acute withdrawal with agitation, vomiting, diaphoresis, hypertension and tachycardia; noncardiogenic pulmonary edema; re-sedation as it wears off
drugs.contraindications: None in life-threatening overdose; use the lowest effective dose in opioid-dependent patients to avoid precipitating severe withdrawal
drugs.tooltip: Duration is only 30 to 90 minutes, shorter than most opioids, so patients must be observed and may need repeat doses or an infusion — especially after methadone or fentanyl analogs.

drugs.name: Flumazenil
drugs.primaryEffect: Reverses benzodiazepine sedation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Reversal of procedural sedation; rarely, isolated benzodiazepine overdose in a benzodiazepine-naive patient
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively antagonizes the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA-A receptor, reversing the potentiation of chloride channel opening frequency.
drugs.sideEffects: Precipitated withdrawal seizures that may be refractory, agitation, arrhythmias, re-sedation as it wears off
drugs.contraindications: Chronic benzodiazepine use or dependence, suspected tricyclic antidepressant co-ingestion, known seizure disorder, unknown polysubstance ingestion
drugs.tooltip: Rarely appropriate in overdose. Removing GABAergic tone in a dependent patient or one who took a tricyclic can trigger seizures that are then untreatable with benzodiazepines.

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.primaryEffect: Reverses muscarinic cholinergic excess
drugs.treatmentUsage: Organophosphate and carbamate poisoning, nerve agent exposure, symptomatic bradycardia, muscarinic mushroom poisoning
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reversing bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, salivation, and gastrointestinal hypermotility; it does not affect nicotinic receptors.
drugs.sideEffects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, tachycardia, hyperthermia, delirium and anticholinergic toxidrome at high doses
drugs.contraindications: None in cholinergic crisis; titrate to drying of bronchial secretions, not to heart rate
drugs.tooltip: Titrate to clearing of pulmonary secretions, since bronchorrhea is what kills. Atropine does nothing for the nicotinic effects — muscle weakness and fasciculations require pralidoxime.

drugs.name: Pralidoxime
drugs.primaryEffect: Regenerates inhibited acetylcholinesterase
drugs.treatmentUsage: Organophosphate and nerve agent poisoning, given together with atropine
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Its oxime group attacks the phosphorus atom bound to acetylcholinesterase, cleaving the organophosphate from the enzyme and restoring its function at both nicotinic and muscarinic synapses.
drugs.sideEffects: Dizziness, blurred vision, headache, tachycardia, hypertension, laryngospasm with rapid infusion
drugs.contraindications: Not useful for carbamate poisoning, which is spontaneously reversible; must be given before aging occurs
drugs.tooltip: Aging is the key concept: the organophosphate-enzyme bond becomes permanent within hours to days, after which pralidoxime cannot work. Give it early and always alongside atropine.

drugs.name: Physostigmine
drugs.primaryEffect: Reverses central and peripheral anticholinergic toxicity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe anticholinergic delirium from antihistamines, jimsonweed, atropine, or belladonna alkaloids
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A tertiary amine that crosses the blood-brain barrier and reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine to outcompete the antimuscarinic agent centrally and peripherally.
drugs.sideEffects: Bradycardia and asystole, seizures, bronchospasm, salivation, vomiting, cholinergic crisis
drugs.contraindications: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose because of asystole risk, QRS widening on ECG, asthma, bowel or bladder obstruction
drugs.tooltip: It crosses into the brain, unlike neostigmine, which is why it treats central delirium. Absolutely avoid in tricyclic overdose where it has caused fatal asystole.

drugs.name: Sodium Bicarbonate
drugs.primaryEffect: Reverses cardiac sodium channel blockade and traps acids in urine
drugs.treatmentUsage: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening, salicylate poisoning, severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia with acidosis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: The sodium load overcomes cardiac sodium channel blockade while alkalinization reduces drug binding to the channel; in salicylate toxicity urinary alkalinization ionizes salicylate and traps it for excretion.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypokalemia, hypernatremia, volume overload, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcemia with tetany, paradoxical CSF acidosis
drugs.contraindications: Alkalemia, severe hypokalemia before repletion, pulmonary edema, hypernatremia
drugs.tooltip: QRS above 100 milliseconds in a tricyclic overdose is the trigger to give bicarbonate. In salicylate toxicity, alkalinizing both blood and urine pulls salicylate out of the brain and into the urine.

drugs.name: Fomepizole
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks conversion of toxic alcohols to their harmful metabolites
drugs.treatmentUsage: Ethylene glycol and methanol poisoning
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase with far greater affinity than ethanol, halting formation of glycolic and oxalic acid from ethylene glycol and formic acid from methanol.
drugs.sideEffects: Headache, nausea, dizziness, transient transaminase elevation, bradycardia, injection site reaction
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; does not eliminate metabolites already formed, so hemodialysis is added for severe acidosis or organ injury
drugs.tooltip: Preferred over ethanol therapy because it needs no level monitoring and does not cause intoxication. Ethylene glycol causes oxalate crystals and renal failure; methanol causes blindness.

drugs.name: Deferoxamine
drugs.primaryEffect: Chelates and eliminates free iron
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acute iron poisoning, chronic transfusional iron overload in thalassemia and sickle cell disease
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A bacterial siderophore that binds free ferric iron with extremely high affinity, forming water-soluble ferrioxamine excreted in urine, giving it a characteristic vin rose color.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypotension with rapid infusion, reddish urine, ototoxicity and retinopathy with chronic use, growth retardation in children, Yersinia and Mucor infection
drugs.contraindications: Severe renal failure or anuria without dialysis; hypersensitivity
drugs.tooltip: Acute iron poisoning has five classic stages, beginning with hemorrhagic gastroenteritis and ending with pyloric scarring. Chelation increases risk of Yersinia and Mucor, which exploit siderophores.

drugs.name: Dimercaprol (BAL)
drugs.primaryEffect: Chelates arsenic, mercury, gold, and lead
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe arsenic, inorganic mercury, and gold poisoning; severe lead encephalopathy with EDTA
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Its two sulfhydryl groups compete with endogenous protein thiol groups for heavy metals, forming a stable ring complex that is excreted renally.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypertension and tachycardia, painful intramuscular injection in peanut oil, nephrotoxicity, fever in children, metallic taste
drugs.contraindications: Peanut allergy because of the oil vehicle, hepatic insufficiency, iron or cadmium poisoning where the complex is more toxic than the metal
drugs.tooltip: British Anti-Lewisite, developed against arsenical war gas. It crosses into the CNS, so it is used first in lead encephalopathy before EDTA to avoid redistributing lead into the brain.

drugs.name: Succimer (DMSA)
drugs.primaryEffect: Oral chelation of lead, arsenic, and mercury
drugs.treatmentUsage: Moderate lead poisoning in children with levels above 45 micrograms per deciliter, arsenic and mercury poisoning
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A water-soluble dimercaprol analog whose sulfhydryl groups bind heavy metals to form stable water-soluble complexes excreted in urine, with far less toxicity than BAL.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, diarrhea, rash, neutropenia, elevated transaminases, metallic taste, mild zinc and copper depletion
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; ongoing lead exposure must be eliminated first or chelation is futile
drugs.tooltip: The oral outpatient chelator for pediatric lead poisoning. Removing the child from the lead source matters more than chelation, which does not reverse established cognitive deficits.

drugs.name: Calcium Disodium EDTA
drugs.primaryEffect: Chelates lead from bone and soft tissue
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe lead poisoning and lead encephalopathy, usually combined with dimercaprol
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Exchanges its calcium for lead to form a stable water-soluble chelate excreted in urine; the calcium salt is used to avoid inducing hypocalcemia.
drugs.sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity with acute tubular necrosis, zinc depletion, fever, hypotension, redistribution of lead into the brain if given alone in encephalopathy
drugs.contraindications: Anuria, active renal disease, lead encephalopathy without prior dimercaprol
drugs.tooltip: In encephalopathy, dimercaprol must be started first — EDTA alone mobilizes lead from bone and can shunt it into the brain, worsening the encephalopathy.

drugs.name: Penicillamine
drugs.primaryEffect: Removes excess copper from tissues
drugs.treatmentUsage: Wilson disease, cystinuria, lead poisoning, historically rheumatoid arthritis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A penicillin metabolite whose sulfhydryl group chelates copper, lead, and mercury, forming soluble complexes excreted in urine; it also complexes cystine to prevent stone formation.
drugs.sideEffects: Nephrotoxicity with membranous nephropathy, aplastic anemia, drug-induced lupus, myasthenia gravis, pemphigus, initial neurologic worsening in Wilson disease, pyridoxine deficiency
drugs.contraindications: Penicillin allergy relative, renal insufficiency, pregnancy, concurrent gold or immunosuppressive therapy
drugs.tooltip: Paradoxical neurologic worsening early in Wilson disease treatment has shifted many toward trientine or zinc. Pyridoxine supplementation is required because penicillamine antagonizes vitamin B6.

drugs.name: Digoxin Immune Fab
drugs.primaryEffect: Binds and neutralizes digoxin in the bloodstream
drugs.treatmentUsage: Digoxin toxicity with life-threatening arrhythmia, hyperkalemia above 5 mEq/L, or hemodynamic instability
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Ovine antibody Fab fragments bind digoxin with higher affinity than the Na-K-ATPase, pulling it off the pump and forming complexes cleared renally.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypokalemia as potassium shifts back intracellularly, recurrence of heart failure or atrial fibrillation, hypersensitivity, falsely elevated total digoxin assays
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in life-threatening toxicity; hypersensitivity to sheep protein is a relative concern
drugs.tooltip: Hyperkalemia in acute digoxin toxicity signals lethality and is the trigger for Fab. Notably, calcium is traditionally avoided in digoxin-related hyperkalemia because of stone heart concerns.

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.primaryEffect: Restores cardiac contractility despite beta blockade
drugs.treatmentUsage: Beta-blocker overdose, calcium channel blocker overdose, severe hypoglycemia, esophageal foreign body
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Activates cardiac Gs-coupled glucagon receptors that raise cAMP through a pathway entirely independent of the beta-adrenergic receptor, restoring inotropy and chronotropy.
drugs.sideEffects: Vomiting with aspiration risk, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, tachyphylaxis at high doses
drugs.contraindications: Pheochromocytoma, insulinoma; protect the airway because vomiting is near-universal at antidotal doses
drugs.tooltip: The classic antidote for beta-blocker overdose precisely because it bypasses the blocked receptor. Doses are far higher than for hypoglycemia, and vomiting is expected — secure the airway.

drugs.name: High-Dose Insulin Euglycemia Therapy
drugs.primaryEffect: Improves myocardial contractility in cardiotoxic overdose
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe calcium channel blocker or beta-blocker overdose with cardiogenic shock
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Supraphysiologic insulin with glucose shifts the poisoned myocardium from fatty acid to carbohydrate metabolism, which it depends on in shock, and provides direct positive inotropy.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, volume overload from dextrose infusion
drugs.contraindications: Requires intensive glucose and potassium monitoring; not appropriate without critical care support
drugs.tooltip: Now considered first-line for severe calcium channel blocker toxicity, ahead of calcium and glucagon. Doses are 10 to 100 times normal, with dextrose and potassium titrated alongside.

drugs.name: Calcium Chloride
drugs.primaryEffect: Overcomes calcium channel blockade and stabilizes the myocardium
drugs.treatmentUsage: Calcium channel blocker overdose, hyperkalemia with ECG changes, hypermagnesemia, hydrofluoric acid exposure
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Raises extracellular calcium to drive calcium influx through remaining unblocked channels and restores the gradient between resting and threshold potential in cardiac myocytes.
drugs.sideEffects: Severe tissue necrosis with extravasation, hypercalcemia, bradycardia, hypotension with rapid push, requires central access
drugs.contraindications: Digoxin toxicity traditionally avoided, hypercalcemia, ventricular fibrillation; never mix with bicarbonate
drugs.tooltip: Calcium chloride has three times the elemental calcium of gluconate but is far more caustic, requiring central access. Gluconate is preferred peripherally.

drugs.name: Intravenous Lipid Emulsion
drugs.primaryEffect: Sequesters lipophilic drugs out of cardiac tissue
drugs.treatmentUsage: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (first-line), refractory cardiotoxicity from other lipophilic drugs such as bupropion or tricyclics
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Creates an intravascular lipid sink that partitions lipophilic drug away from cardiac sodium channels, and provides fatty acid substrate to restore myocardial energy metabolism.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypertriglyceridemia, pancreatitis, fat overload syndrome, interference with laboratory assays, ARDS with large volumes
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to egg or soy; egg allergy is a relative concern in life-threatening toxicity
drugs.tooltip: The rescue for bupivacaine cardiac arrest, which is otherwise notoriously refractory to resuscitation. Prolonged CPR plus lipid emulsion has produced survival after very long arrests.

drugs.name: Hydroxocobalamin
drugs.primaryEffect: Binds circulating cyanide to form vitamin B12
drugs.treatmentUsage: Cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation, industrial exposure, or nitroprusside; refractory vasoplegic shock
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Its cobalt atom binds cyanide with high affinity to form cyanocobalamin, which is nontoxic and renally excreted; it also scavenges nitric oxide, raising blood pressure.
drugs.sideEffects: Red discoloration of skin, urine, and plasma interfering with colorimetric assays and hemodialysis sensors; hypertension; rash; anaphylaxis
drugs.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity; no absolute contraindication in suspected cyanide toxicity
drugs.tooltip: Preferred over nitrite kits in fire victims because it does not induce methemoglobinemia, which would be catastrophic when carbon monoxide already impairs oxygen delivery.

drugs.name: Methylene Blue
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces methemoglobin back to functional hemoglobin
drugs.treatmentUsage: Symptomatic methemoglobinemia from dapsone, benzocaine, nitrites, or aniline dyes; refractory vasoplegic shock
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Serves as an electron acceptor for NADPH methemoglobin reductase, becoming leukomethylene blue which then reduces ferric iron in methemoglobin back to the ferrous oxygen-carrying state.
drugs.sideEffects: Blue-green urine and skin discoloration, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, serotonin syndrome as an MAO inhibitor, paradoxical methemoglobinemia at high doses, falsely low pulse oximetry
drugs.contraindications: G6PD deficiency (it causes hemolysis and does not work), concurrent serotonergic drugs, NADPH methemoglobin reductase deficiency
drugs.tooltip: The classic vignette: cyanosis with normal PaO2 and chocolate-brown blood that does not improve with oxygen. In G6PD deficiency use ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion instead.

drugs.name: Activated Charcoal
drugs.primaryEffect: Adsorbs ingested toxins in the gut before absorption
drugs.treatmentUsage: Recent potentially toxic ingestion, generally within one to two hours; multidose therapy for carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, and theophylline
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Its enormous porous surface area adsorbs toxins by van der Waals forces in the gut lumen, and multidose regimens create a gradient that pulls drug back from the circulation.
drugs.sideEffects: Vomiting, constipation, aspiration pneumonitis which is the feared complication, bowel obstruction with repeated doses, black stools
drugs.contraindications: Unprotected airway or depressed consciousness, bowel obstruction, caustic ingestion, and ingestions it does not bind such as lithium, iron, alcohols, and potassium
drugs.tooltip: Remember what it does not bind with PHAILS: Pesticides, Hydrocarbons, Acids and alkalis, Iron, Lithium, Solvents. Aspiration is the main risk in an obtunded patient.

drugs.name: Leucovorin
drugs.primaryEffect: Bypasses the block on folate metabolism
drugs.treatmentUsage: Methotrexate rescue and overdose, trimethoprim or pyrimethamine toxicity, enhancement of 5-fluorouracil in colorectal cancer
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A reduced folate that enters cells and is converted to tetrahydrofolate downstream of dihydrofolate reductase, restoring thymidine and purine synthesis without needing the blocked enzyme.
drugs.sideEffects: Rash, nausea, hypersensitivity, and paradoxically increased toxicity when combined with 5-fluorouracil where enhancement is intended
drugs.contraindications: Pernicious anemia or vitamin B12 deficiency megaloblastic anemia, where it corrects the blood picture while neurologic damage progresses
drugs.tooltip: It rescues from methotrexate but enhances 5-fluorouracil — opposite effects worth memorizing. Glucarpidase is the alternative rescue that directly cleaves methotrexate in renal failure.

drugs.name: Ethanol (as Antidote)
drugs.primaryEffect: Competitively prevents toxic alcohol metabolism
drugs.treatmentUsage: Ethylene glycol and methanol poisoning when fomepizole is unavailable
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competes for alcohol dehydrogenase with roughly 10 to 20 times greater affinity than methanol or ethylene glycol, preventing their conversion to toxic acid metabolites.
drugs.sideEffects: Intoxication, sedation, respiratory depression, hypoglycemia especially in children, hyponatremia, phlebitis with intravenous infusion
drugs.contraindications: Concurrent disulfiram or metronidazole, hepatic failure; requires frequent ethanol level monitoring
drugs.tooltip: Largely replaced by fomepizole, which requires no level monitoring and does not sedate. Ethanol remains a valid option where fomepizole is unavailable or unaffordable.

drugs.name: Octreotide (Sulfonylurea Overdose)
drugs.primaryEffect: Suppresses insulin release in sulfonylurea toxicity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Refractory hypoglycemia from sulfonylurea overdose that recurs despite dextrose
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds somatostatin receptors on pancreatic beta cells, hyperpolarizing them via potassium channel activation and blocking the calcium-dependent insulin secretion that sulfonylureas drive.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, abdominal cramping, hyperglycemia, bradycardia, gallstones with prolonged use, injection site pain
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; caution in diabetes; does not replace dextrose for immediate correction
drugs.tooltip: Dextrose alone can worsen sulfonylurea hypoglycemia by stimulating further insulin release. Octreotide breaks that cycle and is the definitive treatment for recurrent episodes.

drugs.name: Dantrolene
drugs.primaryEffect: Halts sustained skeletal muscle contraction and heat generation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Malignant hyperthermia (first-line), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, severe spasticity
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the RYR1 ryanodine receptor on skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum, blocking calcium release so excitation-contraction coupling and the resulting hypermetabolism stop.
drugs.sideEffects: Muscle weakness, sedation, dizziness, hepatotoxicity with chronic use, respiratory depression, phlebitis
drugs.contraindications: Chronic use in active hepatic disease; not effective for cardiac or smooth muscle
drugs.tooltip: Triggered by succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics in susceptible patients with RYR1 mutations. Rising end-tidal CO2 is the earliest sign, before temperature rises.

drugs.name: Cyproheptadine
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks serotonin receptors in serotonin syndrome
drugs.treatmentUsage: Moderate to severe serotonin syndrome not responding to benzodiazepines and supportive care; appetite stimulation
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Antagonizes 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A receptors along with H1 histamine receptors, reversing the excessive serotonergic stimulation causing hyperthermia, clonus, and agitation.
drugs.sideEffects: Sedation, anticholinergic effects, weight gain, dry mouth, urinary retention
drugs.contraindications: Narrow-angle glaucoma, bladder outlet obstruction, elderly patients; oral only, so an unprotected airway limits use
drugs.tooltip: Distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome: serotonin syndrome has clonus, hyperreflexia, and rapid onset in hours; NMS has lead-pipe rigidity and evolves over days.

drugs.name: Naltrexone
drugs.primaryEffect: Long-acting blockade of opioid receptors
drugs.treatmentUsage: Relapse prevention in opioid use disorder, alcohol use disorder, cholestatic pruritus
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively antagonizes mu opioid receptors for 24 to 72 hours, blocking both exogenous opioid euphoria and endogenous opioid-mediated reward from alcohol.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, headache, hepatotoxicity at high doses, precipitated withdrawal, complete blockade of opioid analgesia in emergencies
drugs.contraindications: Current opioid use or dependence, acute hepatitis or hepatic failure, anticipated need for opioid analgesia
drugs.tooltip: Distinguish from naloxone: naltrexone is long-acting oral or monthly injectable for maintenance, whereas naloxone is short-acting for acute overdose reversal.

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.primaryEffect: Prevents and treats Wernicke encephalopathy
drugs.treatmentUsage: Wernicke encephalopathy, alcohol use disorder, refeeding syndrome prophylaxis, wet beriberi with high-output heart failure
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Vitamin B1 is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase; deficiency cripples aerobic glucose metabolism in high-demand neurons.
drugs.sideEffects: Very well tolerated; rare anaphylaxis with intravenous administration, injection site irritation
drugs.contraindications: Essentially none; give before or with glucose in any at-risk patient
drugs.tooltip: Give thiamine before glucose in alcoholic or malnourished patients, because a glucose load consumes remaining thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

drugs.name: Vitamin K (Phytonadione)
drugs.primaryEffect: Restores production of clotting factors
drugs.treatmentUsage: Warfarin overdose or supratherapeutic INR, superwarfarin rodenticide ingestion, vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Provides the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to carboxylate factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S, restoring their ability to bind calcium and phospholipid.
drugs.sideEffects: Anaphylactoid reactions with rapid intravenous administration, flushing, warfarin resistance for up to two weeks after high doses
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; intravenous doses must be given slowly and diluted
drugs.tooltip: Superwarfarin rodenticides have half-lives of weeks to months and can require oral vitamin K for many months. Life-threatening bleeding needs 4-factor PCC for immediate factor replacement.

drugs.name: Hyperbaric Oxygen
drugs.primaryEffect: Accelerates carbon monoxide elimination
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe carbon monoxide poisoning with loss of consciousness, neurologic deficit, cardiac ischemia, or pregnancy; decompression sickness; necrotizing infections
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Raises dissolved plasma oxygen dramatically and shortens the carboxyhemoglobin half-life from about 5 hours on room air to roughly 20 minutes, while also reducing lipid peroxidation.
drugs.sideEffects: Barotrauma to the ears and sinuses, oxygen toxicity seizures, pulmonary edema, claustrophobia, reversible myopia
drugs.contraindications: Untreated pneumothorax (absolute), certain chemotherapy agents such as bleomycin, severe COPD with carbon dioxide retention
drugs.tooltip: Pulse oximetry is falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning because it cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin — co-oximetry is required for diagnosis.

drugs.name: Glucarpidase
drugs.primaryEffect: Rapidly degrades circulating methotrexate
drugs.treatmentUsage: Toxic methotrexate levels with delayed clearance due to acute kidney injury
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A recombinant bacterial carboxypeptidase that cleaves methotrexate into inactive glutamate and DAMPA, reducing plasma levels by over 95 percent within 15 minutes.
drugs.sideEffects: Paresthesias, flushing, nausea, headache, hypersensitivity, antibody formation, interference with methotrexate immunoassays
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; leucovorin must be separated by at least two hours because glucarpidase also cleaves it
drugs.tooltip: Because it works only extracellularly, leucovorin must still be continued to rescue cells. Dosing leucovorin within two hours of glucarpidase destroys it, which is a critical timing point.

drugs.name: Idarucizumab
drugs.primaryEffect: Immediately reverses dabigatran anticoagulation
drugs.treatmentUsage: Life-threatening bleeding on dabigatran or the need for emergency surgery
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with roughly 350 times the affinity of thrombin, sequestering it into an inactive complex cleared renally.
drugs.sideEffects: Thrombotic events once anticoagulation is removed, hypokalemia, headache, hypersensitivity, rebound anticoagulation in some patients
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; hereditary fructose intolerance because of the sorbitol excipient
drugs.tooltip: Reverses within minutes, the first truly specific direct oral anticoagulant antidote. Anticoagulation should be restarted as soon as bleeding is controlled, given the underlying thrombotic risk.

drugs.name: Pyridoxine
drugs.primaryEffect: Terminates seizures from isoniazid toxicity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Isoniazid overdose with refractory seizures, gyromitra mushroom poisoning, prevention of isoniazid neuropathy, hydrazine exposure
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxal 5-phosphate, the cofactor for glutamic acid decarboxylase, so GABA cannot be synthesized; repleting pyridoxine restores GABA production and stops seizures.
drugs.sideEffects: Sensory peripheral neuropathy with chronic high-dose use, nausea, headache, sedation at very high doses
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; chronic megadoses cause a paradoxical sensory neuropathy
drugs.tooltip: Isoniazid seizures are refractory to benzodiazepines alone because the problem is absent GABA synthesis, not receptor function. Give gram-for-gram pyridoxine matching the isoniazid ingested.

drugs.name: Phentolamine
drugs.primaryEffect: Reverses alpha-mediated vasoconstriction
drugs.treatmentUsage: Extravasation of vasopressors, cocaine-induced hypertension and coronary vasospasm, pheochromocytoma hypertensive crisis, hypertensive crisis from MAO inhibitor and tyramine interaction
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Nonselective competitive alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic antagonist that produces immediate vasodilation, reversing catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction.
drugs.sideEffects: Reflex tachycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, flushing, nasal congestion, angina
drugs.contraindications: Myocardial infarction and coronary insufficiency relative, hypotension
drugs.tooltip: In cocaine toxicity, unopposed beta blockade can worsen coronary vasospasm through unopposed alpha stimulation, so benzodiazepines and phentolamine are used instead of beta-blockers.

drugs.name: Sodium Thiosulfate
drugs.primaryEffect: Converts cyanide to a nontoxic excretable form
drugs.treatmentUsage: Cyanide poisoning, nitroprusside toxicity, calciphylaxis, cisplatin ototoxicity prevention
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Donates sulfur to the mitochondrial enzyme rhodanese, which transfers it to cyanide forming thiocyanate, a far less toxic compound cleared by the kidneys.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea and vomiting, hypotension, thiocyanate toxicity with confusion and seizures in renal failure, metabolic acidosis
drugs.contraindications: Caution in renal impairment where thiocyanate accumulates; slower onset than hydroxocobalamin
drugs.tooltip: Historically paired with sodium nitrite, which induces methemoglobin to bind cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin has displaced the nitrite-thiosulfate kit in smoke inhalation because it does not impair oxygen carrying.

drugs.name: Protamine Sulfate
drugs.primaryEffect: Neutralizes heparin
drugs.treatmentUsage: Heparin overdose with bleeding, reversal after cardiopulmonary bypass or vascular surgery
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A strongly cationic protein derived from fish sperm that binds ionically to anionic heparin, forming a stable inactive complex that is cleared from the circulation.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypotension, bradycardia, anaphylaxis, pulmonary hypertension, paradoxical anticoagulation when given in excess
drugs.contraindications: Prior severe protamine reaction; heightened risk in fish allergy, prior NPH insulin exposure, and after vasectomy
drugs.tooltip: Reverses unfractionated heparin completely, low molecular weight heparin only partially, and fondaparinux not at all. Excess protamine paradoxically prolongs bleeding.
